1.open: When you hear bad news about someone you care about who lives far away, what is the first thing you tend to do?
questions: The visitors report that the people are "in great trouble and disgrace" and the wall is "broken down" (v. 3). Why would a broken wall matter so much to people living in a city then?
Nehemiah lives in a palace, far from Jerusalem, and could have shrugged this off. Why do you think the news hit him so hard?
He "sat down and wept" and mourned for days (v. 4). When did you last grieve over something that wasn't happening to you personally? What was that like?
Before he asks for anything, Nehemiah describes God as "the great and awesome God who keeps His covenant of loving devotion" (v. 5). How does starting with who God is change the way a person prays?
He confesses, "Both I and my father's house have sinned" (v. 6). He does not blame others and he includes himself. What makes that kind of honesty hard, and what might it make possible?
In verses 8 and 9 Nehemiah reminds God of a promise that scattered people would be gathered if they returned. How does remembering what God has said help when a situation looks bleak?
Nehemiah prays for "success this day" and mercy "in the sight of this man," and only then do we learn the man is the king (v. 11). What do you notice about someone who prays first and acts second?
Maybe you have prayed about something for a long time and seen no change, or you are not sure prayer does anything. What would an honest prayer from you sound like right now?
1.life: Pick one person, place or situation you care about that feels out of your hands. Each day this week, pray for it by name, starting with a line about who God is and then telling him the truth, including where you may have played a part.
1.prayer: Thank God that he listens, and that he keeps his promises. Bring to him one broken situation the group cares about, and ask what part, if any, he may be inviting you to play.
1.tip: Verses 6 and 7 can make people uneasy, because confessing sins that you did not personally commit feels odd. Keep it simple: Nehemiah stands with his people instead of standing above them. Invite the group to talk about what it looks like to own a shared problem without sinking into guilt.

2.open: Think of a project you started, like fixing something at home or organizing something for a group. What made you finally begin?
questions: The king asks, "Why is your face sad, though you are not ill?" (v. 2). Nehemiah says he was "overwhelmed with fear." Why would a sad face be risky in front of a Persian king, and when have you felt afraid to let someone see what was really going on with you?

When the king asks, "What is your request?" Nehemiah writes, "So I prayed to the God of heaven" (v. 4). What do you notice about a prayer that is that short and that quick? When have you prayed like that?

Nehemiah asks for time off, letters for safe passage, and timber (vv. 5-8). What does it tell you that he planned his request so carefully, and that he still says it happened because "the gracious hand of my God was upon me" (v. 8)?

Sanballat and Tobiah were "deeply disturbed that someone had come to seek the well-being of the Israelites" (v. 10). Why might some people be upset when something good is about to happen? Have you ever seen that?

Nehemiah spent three days in Jerusalem, then went out at night and told no one what "my God had laid on my heart" (vv. 11-12). Why might he have looked things over first before speaking? What do you do before you share a big idea or concern?
Nehemiah tells the people, "You see the trouble we are in" (v. 17). Why does it matter to name the problem out loud together before trying to fix it?

After he shares his story, the people reply, "Let us start rebuilding," and "they set their hands to this good work" (v. 18). What is one thing in your church, family or neighborhood that feels broken, and what would it look like to put your hands to it?

Some people read this chapter as a model of wise leadership, and others as mainly a story of God quietly working through a foreign king. If you are honest, where do you find it hard to believe God is working behind the scenes in your life right now?
2.life: Pick one broken thing you care about, such as a relationship, a ministry or a corner of your neighborhood. This week, pray a short prayer about it each day, then take one small step, like looking it over honestly or asking one person to help.
2.prayer: Thank God that he notices what breaks our hearts and is not bothered by our short, scared prayers. Ask for courage to start, patience to look carefully, and good people to work beside.
2.tip: The last question may stir up doubt or feelings of being unseen by God. Don't rush to fix it. Let people answer honestly, and remind the group that Nehemiah's story began with four months of waiting and grief before this chapter.

3.open: Think of a time you helped with a big group project, like a move, a church event or a community cleanup. What was your job, and what do you remember about it?
questions: This chapter is mostly a list of names and places. Why do you think the writer recorded who built which section, instead of just saying the wall was rebuilt?
The high priest and his fellow priests started at the Sheep Gate, and "they dedicated it" (v. 1). Why might it matter that the work began with the priests and with dedicating it to God?
Goldsmiths, perfumers, rulers and ordinary families all worked on the wall (vv. 8, 9, 12). What does it say about God's people that these very different people shared one job?

Several people repaired the wall "opposite his house" or "in front of his own house" (vv. 29, 28). What is the value of working on the piece closest to your own home? What is your version of that today?
Verse 12 says Shallum worked "with the help of his daughters." What might it mean that this detail was remembered? Who in your life works quietly in the background?
"Their nobles did not put their shoulders to the work" (v. 5). Why might someone hold back from shared work? Be honest: when have you held back, and what was behind it?

Baruch "diligently repaired another section" (v. 20), and Meremoth took on a second section (v. 21). When have you seen someone give more than what was asked, and how did it affect the people around them?
If our group were one section of a wall, what part of the work do you think God has put in front of us right now? If you are not sure where you fit, or whether you do, what would help?
3.life: Pick one small, practical job this week that serves someone near you, such as a neighbor, your church or your family, and do it without being asked. Then thank someone whose quiet work usually goes unnoticed.
3.prayer: Thank God that he knows each of our names and our small contributions. Ask him to show each person in the group where to put a hand to the work, and for a willing spirit to do it.
3.tip: A chapter of names can feel dull, so people may go quiet. Read it aloud briefly, then move straight to the questions about the people (Shallum's daughters, Baruch, the Tekoite nobles). Handle the Tekoite question gently: aim it at our own reasons for holding back, not at judging others.

4.open: What is a project you started that took much longer or was much harder than you expected?
questions: Sanballat and Tobiah mock the builders with questions like "Can they restore the wall by themselves?" (v. 2). Why does mockery hurt so much, and when have you felt it for something you cared about?

Nehemiah responds to the insults with a raw prayer, asking God to turn their scorn back on their own heads (vv. 4-5). The text records it without comment. What do you make of praying that honestly when you are angry or hurt?
Verse 6 says the wall went up "for the people had a mind to work." What helps you keep going on something hard when the finish line is far away?
In verse 10 the workers say, "The strength of the laborer fails, and there is so much rubble." Where do you feel worn out right now, and what does the rubble look like in your life?
Verse 9 says, "we prayed to our God and posted a guard." Why might the chapter put prayer and practical action side by side? Where do you tend to lean on one more than the other?

Nehemiah tells the people, "Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome, and fight for your brothers, your sons and your daughters, your wives and your homes" (v. 14). What helps you remember who God is when you are afraid?
The builders work "with one hand" while holding a weapon "with the other" (v. 17), and Nehemiah says, "Our God will fight for us!" (v. 20). How do you hold together trusting God and doing your part?

Think about the people along the wall, spread out far from one another, who needed to hear the horn and come together (vv. 19-20). Who helps you keep going, and who might need you to show up for them? If you are not sure you have anyone, what would help?
4.life: Think of one hard thing you have been tempted to quit. This week, pray about it each day and ask one person to check in on you, so you do not carry it alone.
4.prayer: Be honest with God about what is wearing you out or what you are afraid of. Ask him to help you remember that he is "great and awesome" (v. 14), and pray for someone in the group who feels tired.
4.tip: Verses 4 and 5 are an angry prayer, and verses 13 to 18 involve weapons, so someone may ask whether the chapter endorses revenge or violence. Keep it simple: the text records what Nehemiah prayed and did without calling it a model for everything. Point the group to the main thread, which is prayer, watchfulness, and working together under pressure.

5.open: Have you ever lent something to a friend or family member, like money, a tool or a car, and wondered if you would get it back? What happened?
questions: The people say, "We must get grain in order to eat and stay alive" (v. 2). What pressures are the families in this chapter facing, and which of them would feel familiar to people today?
In verse 5 the poor say they are "just like our countrymen and their children," yet their children are being enslaved. Why do you think this part of their protest matters so much to them?
Nehemiah says, "I became extremely angry," and then acted "after serious thought" (v. 6). What do you notice about how he handles his anger? When has anger helped you or hurt you?
Nehemiah points out that they had bought back Jews sold to foreigners, but now were selling their own (v. 8). How can people do something good in one area and miss the same thing close to home?
He asks, "Shouldn't you walk in the fear of our God" (v. 9). What do you think it means to let your respect for God shape how you handle money and power?

The lenders have nothing to say (v. 8), but then they agree to give everything back (v. 12). Why might a public promise help someone keep their word? When has being held accountable been good for you?

Nehemiah says he did not claim the governor's food allowance "because of my fear of God" (v. 15). Where have you seen someone use their position to serve others rather than take what they were entitled to?
Nehemiah ends by asking God, "Remember me favorably" (v. 19). How do you feel about asking God to notice the good you do? If that feels awkward or hard to believe, what makes it so?
5.life: Think of one place where you have some power or advantage, such as money, a job, a skill or a reputation. This week, take one concrete step to use it for someone who has less, and do it quietly.
5.prayer: Ask God to open your eyes to people who are struggling under heavy burdens. Pray for the courage to act fairly and generously where you have influence.
5.tip: This chapter can slide into arguments about modern lending, interest and politics. Gently steer back to what the text shows: the cry of the poor, leaders held accountable, and Nehemiah's own example. Let people share personal experiences with debt, but don't let anyone be made to feel shamed for their financial situation.

6.open: What is something you started that you were tempted to quit halfway through, and what kept you going?
questions: Nehemiah answers the invitation to Ono with, "I am doing a great work and cannot come down" (v. 3). What helps you stay focused on what matters when something else is pulling at your time?
Sanballat sent the same message four times, and Nehemiah gave the same reply each time (v. 4). Why might repeated pressure be harder to resist than a single big temptation?
The fifth message was an open letter spreading a rumor that Nehemiah planned to make himself king (vv. 6-7). Why would a false accusation like that be so dangerous, then and now?
Verse 9 says the enemies wanted to frighten the builders, and Nehemiah prays, "my God, strengthen my hands." When have you prayed a short, plain prayer like that? What was happening?

Shemaiah urged Nehemiah to hide in the temple, but Nehemiah asked, "Should one like me go into the temple to save his own life?" (v. 11). Why would this have been a trap, even though it looked like a religious and safe choice?
Nehemiah realized that "God had not sent him" (v. 12). How can we test whether advice that sounds spiritual really comes from God? Who helps you do that?
Verse 16 says the surrounding nations "realized that this task had been accomplished by our God." Where have you seen something finished that you could not have done on your own?

Verses 17 to 19 show that some of Nehemiah's own people were friendly with Tobiah and kept reporting back to him. If you feel unsure about what to make of this, or even unsure about God, what is one honest thing you would say about how you handle pressure from people close to you?
6.life: Think of one good thing you are doing that you feel pressure to drop. This week, name the pressure honestly, ask one trusted person for their view, and pray Nehemiah's words: "strengthen my hands" (v. 9).
6.prayer: Ask God for steady hands and a clear mind when pressure, rumors or fear show up. Pray for wisdom to tell a true warning from a voice meant to wear you down.
6.tip: Verses 17 to 19 can feel like a list of names with little point, and some may wonder why they are here. Keep it short: even inside the community, loyalties were divided, and Nehemiah had to stay faithful without knowing who to trust. If the group runs long on earlier questions, you can skip to the last question and let people answer honestly, including those who feel unsure.

7.open: Do you know the story of how your family ended up in the place where you live now? Share a little of it, or a story you wish you knew.
questions: Nehemiah picks Hanani and Hananiah because Hananiah was "a faithful man who feared God more than most" (v. 2). What qualities would you look for in someone you trusted with something important, and which of them can you grow in yourself?
Nehemiah tells the guards, "Do not open the gates of Jerusalem until the sun is hot" (v. 3). Why might finishing a big project still leave you with work to do to protect it?
Verse 4 says "the city was large and spacious, but there were few people in it." Have you ever finished something, like a move, a job or a goal, and still felt it was empty? What was missing?
Nehemiah says, "my God put it into my heart" to register the people (v. 5). What do you make of the idea that God prompts ordinary leaders to do plain, practical tasks like this one?
Most of this chapter is names, families and numbers, such as "the descendants of Parosh, 2,172" (v. 8). What does it say about God and his people that every family is counted and remembered?

Some families "could not prove that their families were descended from Israel" (v. 61), and some priests were excluded when they could not find their records (v. 64). How does it feel to read about people left outside because of missing paperwork? How might this land for someone who has ever felt like they did not quite belong?

The people gave gold, silver and priestly garments for the work (vv. 70 to 72), and then everyone settled in their towns (v. 73). What do you notice about how this community shared the load, and where do you see a version of that in our own group?
7.life: Nehemiah turned to the people after the wall was done. This week, reach out to one person who is on the edge of your group, church or neighborhood, and learn their name and a bit of their story.
7.prayer: Thank God that he knows every person by name and that no one is lost in the crowd. Ask him to show you who in your life needs to be noticed and welcomed.
7.tip: A chapter of names and numbers can feel like a slog, so do not read it all aloud. Read the opening and closing sections, give a one-line summary of the lists in between, and spend your time on the questions about belonging and being known.

8.open: What is a time you heard or read something that you had been missing for a long time, like a letter, a recipe or a song, and it stopped you in your tracks?
questions: The people themselves "asked Ezra the scribe to bring out the Book of the Law" (v. 1). What do you think made them want to hear it? What makes you want, or not want, to open the Bible?
Ezra read "from daybreak until noon" and "all the people listened attentively" (v. 3). What helps you listen well, and what gets in the way when you read or hear Scripture?

When Ezra opened the book, "all the people stood up," and then they said "Amen, Amen!" and bowed with their faces to the ground (vv. 5, 6). What do our bodies and habits in worship say about how we treat God's word?
The Levites read "explaining it and giving insight, so that the people could understand what was being read" (v. 8). Who has helped you understand the Bible, and how could we do that for each other?
"All the people were weeping as they heard the words of the Law" (v. 9). Why do you think they wept? Has hearing something true about yourself ever brought grief and relief together?

Nehemiah says, "Go and eat what is rich, drink what is sweet, and send out portions to those who have nothing prepared" (v. 10). Why might God's people be sent to a feast after tears? Who in your life could use a portion this week?
"The joy of the LORD is your strength" (v. 10). What does that look like on a hard day? If joy feels far away right now, what is that like for you, and what would you honestly say about it?
The people found a command they had forgotten, then did it, and "there was great rejoicing" (vv. 14 to 17). Is there something in Scripture you know about but have never really put into practice?
8.life: Pick one short passage and read it slowly each day this week, once out loud. Ask one person you trust what it means to them. Then do one small, concrete thing it points to, like sharing a meal with someone who is alone.
8.prayer: Thank God for giving us his word and for people who help us understand it. Ask him to meet you in both your sorrow and your joy, and to help you hear his word with hope, not dread.
8.tip: Verse 10 can sound like a command to cheer up, which can hurt someone who is grieving or doubting. Point out that the leaders were not scolding the people for feeling sorry. They were pointing them to the good news of a holy day, so make space for honest feelings before talking about joy.

9.open: What is something you keep meaning to fix or clear out, and what usually gets in the way?
questions: The people fast, wear sackcloth and put dust on their heads (v. 1). Why might people use their bodies to show sorrow, and what do we do today that serves the same purpose?
They spent about a quarter of the day hearing the law read and another quarter in "confession and worship" (v. 3). What do you notice about hearing God's word first and confessing second?
The prayer begins with who God is before it says anything about the people: "You alone are the LORD" (v. 6). How does starting with God change the way we pray about our failures?
Verse 17 says, "You are a forgiving God, gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and rich in loving devotion." Which of those words is easiest for you to believe about God, and which is hardest?
Even after the calf idol, "You in Your great compassion did not forsake them" (vv. 18, 19). What does it mean to you that God kept guiding them when they did not deserve it?
Verse 25 says that in the good land "they ate and were filled; they grew fat," and then verse 26 says they rebelled. Why can comfort be as risky to our faith as hardship?
Verses 26 to 31 describe a cycle: rebellion, trouble, a cry for help, rescue, and then rebellion again. Where do you see a cycle like that in your own life or in the church today?

The prayer ends with "here we are as slaves" (v. 36), and still they commit to a written agreement (v. 38). If you feel stuck or unsure whether God is listening, what do you want to say to him honestly?
9.life: Set aside fifteen minutes this week to read through a part of your own story, like the last year or a long season, as this prayer does. Write down where you saw God's patience, and one pattern you want to bring to him honestly.
9.prayer: Thank God that he is "gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and rich in loving devotion." Ask him to help you name your own patterns without fear, and to trust his mercy more than your own record.
9.tip: Verse 24 celebrates the Canaanites being handed over to Israel, and some people will find that hard to read. Acknowledge it plainly, note that the prayer is the people's own retelling of their history, and bring the group back to the chapter's main thread: God's patience and the people's honest confession.

10.open: What is a promise you made, like a New Year's resolution or a commitment to a friend, that you really meant at the time?
questions: The chapter opens with a long list of names, starting with "Nehemiah the governor" (v. 1). Why might it matter that real names were written down, and that the leaders signed first?
The people "commit themselves with a sworn oath to follow the Law of God" (v. 29). What does putting a promise in writing and signing it in public add that a private intention does not?
The oath includes wives and children "who are able to understand" (v. 28). Who helped you understand your faith when you were younger, and what did they do that made a difference?

Verse 30 says, "We will not give our daughters in marriage to the people of the land." The aim was to protect their faith, but it also shut some people out. Christians read and apply this in different ways. How do you think about the balance between protecting faith and welcoming outsiders?
They promise not to buy on the Sabbath and to "cancel every debt" every seventh year (v. 31). How do rest and care for people in debt show up as faith, not just as rules?

Much of the chapter is about money, food and wood for the temple, ending with "we will not neglect the house of our God" (v. 39). What does it look like today to support the place and people where you worship, with time, money or skills?

Chapter 13 shows the people slipped on several of these promises. Where have you made a sincere promise to God and then struggled to keep it? What would an honest conversation with God about that sound like?
Some Christians see this pledge as a model of wholehearted recommitment, and others see it as a sincere effort that shows the limits of keeping God's law by promises alone. What do you take from it?
10.life: Choose one small, specific commitment to God or to your church family, such as a regular time of prayer, a gift, or an act of service. Write it down, tell one person in the group, and ask them to check in with you next week.
10.prayer: Thank God that he is faithful even when we are not. Ask for honesty about the promises you have made and help to keep the ones that matter.
10.tip: The list of names and the offering details can feel dull or distant, and verse 30 on marriage can stir strong feelings. Read only the suggested verses, spend a moment on why names and specifics matter, and for verse 30 say plainly that Christians read it differently and that it caused real pain elsewhere in this book. Then move on to the question about promises.

11.open: Have you ever moved somewhere new, or helped someone else move? What was the hardest part?
questions: The people cast lots so that one in ten would move into the city, while the other nine stayed in their own towns (v. 1). Why do you think they chose a method that left the decision to God instead of picking people themselves?
Moving to Jerusalem likely meant leaving family land for a poorer, more exposed city. What do you think it cost the ones who were chosen, and what might it have cost the ones who stayed behind?
"The people blessed all the men who volunteered to live in Jerusalem" (v. 2). Who in your life or church gives up something quietly, and how could we thank them out loud?
Much of this chapter is names, family lines and numbers. What does it say about God and his people that these ordinary people are written down one by one?

Some of the people listed were gatekeepers, singers and workers on the outside tasks of the temple (vv. 16, 19, 22). Which of these jobs would you most likely have had, and why does the work behind the scenes matter?
Mattaniah "led in thanksgiving and prayer" (v. 17). When is it hardest for you to give thanks, and what helps when it feels forced or empty?
Honestly, how do you feel about being asked to give up comfort or convenience for the sake of a community? If the answer is mixed or you are not sure, that is welcome here.
When a group needs some people to sacrifice for the common good, what makes the way they are chosen feel fair or unfair to you?
11.life: Look for one person who serves in a quiet, unseen way in your church, family or neighborhood. This week, thank them by name, either in person or in a note.
11.prayer: Thank God that he knows each person by name and values every kind of service. Ask for a willing heart to give something up for others, and for eyes to notice those who already do.
11.tip: A chapter of names and numbers can make a group's eyes glaze over, so read only the passages listed and don't try to cover every verse. Spend your time on the volunteers and the unseen workers. Also, the chapter does not say how the lots were drawn or how people felt about moving, so avoid guessing too confidently and keep questions about cost open and honest.

12.open: What is something your family or friends always celebrate together, and what makes it feel special?
questions: Most of this chapter is a list of names. Why might the writer have wanted these people remembered, and how do you feel when you read a list like this?

Verse 24 says the Levites stood across from each other "to give praise and thanksgiving as one section alternated with the other." What does it say about worship that it was organized and shared, not just done alone?

Before the celebration, the priests and Levites "purified themselves," then the people, the gates and the wall (v. 30). The text does not say exactly how. What do you think it means to set something apart for God before celebrating?

Nehemiah split the people into two choirs walking opposite ways around the wall until they met at the temple (vv. 31, 38, 40). What do you notice about how this picture shows people working and rejoicing together?
Verse 43 says "God had given them great joy," and the sound of it "was heard from afar." When has joy in your own life been bigger than you expected, or harder to feel than you wanted?
The wall took great effort and faced real opposition, and now they stop to give thanks. What is something you have finished or come through that you have never really stopped to thank God for?

Verse 44 says Judah "rejoiced over the priests and Levites who were serving," and they set up storerooms to support them. Who serves quietly in your church or community, and how could you show them appreciation in a practical way?
If joy feels distant for you right now, or you are unsure about all this celebrating, what honestly comes to mind when you read about a whole city rejoicing?
12.life: Think of one person who serves behind the scenes at your church or in your community. This week, thank them in a specific way, with a note, a meal or a gift of your time.
12.prayer: Thank God for something he has helped you finish or get through, and ask him to give your group a joy that is shared and not just private.
12.tip: The long lists of names can make people's eyes glaze over, so don't read them all aloud. Read verses 1 to 9 and then move on, and say plainly that the names show God's people were remembered one by one. Spend your time on the celebration in verses 27 to 43.

13.open: What is something you started with great energy, like a habit or a project, that slowly slipped once life got busy?
questions: Nehemiah comes back and finds that the temple storeroom has been given to Tobiah, an outsider who had opposed him (vv. 4-7). How does something important get slowly crowded out of a church, a family or a life without anyone deciding to do it?

Nehemiah asks the officials, "Why has the house of God been neglected?" (v. 11). The Levites had left because they were not being paid. What does that tell us about how everyday support and care keep worship going?
In verse 13 Nehemiah appoints treasurers "because they were considered trustworthy." Who has been trustworthy in your church or community, and what difference have they made?

The people were buying and selling on the Sabbath, and Nehemiah shut the gates (vv. 15-19). What did the Sabbath protect for Israel then? What would real rest look like for you, and what gets in the way?
Three times Nehemiah prays, "Remember me" (vv. 14, 22, 31). What do you hear in those prayers: confidence, worry, or something else? How do you think God hears them?

In verses 23 to 27 Nehemiah is worried that the children no longer speak the language of Judah and that Solomon was drawn into sin. He also beats some of the men and pulls out their hair (v. 25). What do you make of his methods? Christians read this differently: some see faithful zeal for that moment, others see a harsh response that books like Ruth and Jonah seem to push against.
The study note asks where the line is between protecting what matters and shutting people out. Where have you seen a community get that balance right, or wrong?

Nehemiah fixes a lot in this chapter, yet the book ends with him asking for God's favor, not claiming it (v. 31). If you are honest, do you feel more like someone who has it together or someone still needing mercy? What would you say to God about that?
13.life: Pick one thing that has slipped, such as a habit of prayer, a regular rest day, or support for someone who serves your church. Take one small, specific step to restore it this week, and ask God for mercy where you have let it go.
13.prayer: Ask God to show where good things have been neglected and to give steady, gentle faithfulness to restore them. Ask for mercy "according to Your abundant loving devotion" (v. 22), and for wisdom to protect what matters without shutting people out.
13.tip: Verses 25 to 28 are hard, and the group may be uncomfortable or tempted to excuse or condemn Nehemiah quickly. Say plainly that Christians read this differently, and that the Bible reports what he did without calling every action a model. Then steer back to the chapter's wider themes: neglect, trust and the need for mercy.
